opus-5.5.text:
I think they really reinforce each other. The frontier models are where you push the boundaries of what's possible — you find out what new capabilities emerge when you scale up compute, data, and model size, and you learn a lot about which training techniques and architectural ideas actually work. But those very large models are expensive to serve, and you can't put them in front of billions of users for every query, or run them with the low latency a lot of applications need.

So one of the things we've found really effective is using the frontier model as a teacher. Distillation is an idea I worked on with Geoffrey Hinton and Oriol Vinyals years ago. You take the rich output distribution of a big, capable model and use it to train a much smaller model. The smaller model ends up far better than if you'd trained it from scratch on the same data, because it's getting a much richer signal than just the hard labels. That's a big part of how you get something like a Flash model that's remarkably capable but cheap and fast enough to deploy really broadly.

And it goes the other way too. When lots of people are using the smaller, affordable models, you learn what they actually use them for, where they fall short, and which capabilities matter most in practice. That feeds back into what you prioritize for the next frontier model. Making the small models efficient also pushes you to get better at things like quantization, serving infrastructure, and hardware co-design, and those benefit the big models as well.

So I don't see it as a trade-off between one or the other. You need the frontier to keep advancing what's possible, and you need the efficient models to make those advances actually useful to as many people as possible. Each generation of the big model makes the next generation of small models better, and that's been a pretty powerful cycle.

r001.rationale: It says large models cannot serve applications requiring low latency, making smaller, fast models useful.

r002.rationale: It explains that a frontier model can teach a smaller model through distillation, improving it beyond training from scratch.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think they really feed each other. The frontier models are where you find out what's possible. You push on scale, on data, on new architectural ideas, and you discover capabilities that nobody quite predicted. That's the research edge, and it's genuinely important to keep pushing it, because the ceiling keeps moving.

But the thing is, most of the uses people actually want don't need the biggest model you can build. If you're doing something a billion times a day, you care enormously about cost, latency, and energy per query. And it turns out a lot of what the frontier model learns can be transferred down. Distillation is the obvious example: you use the big model as a teacher, and you get a much smaller model that captures a surprising fraction of the capability at a tiny fraction of the cost. So the frontier work is almost the raw material for the small models.

It goes the other direction too. Working on efficient models forces you to think hard about what's actually essential, about systems, about hardware, about sparsity and quantization and serving. A lot of those ideas then flow back up into how you train and serve the large models. When you're training at the scale of a frontier model, every efficiency win is worth a lot.

And from a product standpoint, you want the whole spectrum. Some tasks genuinely need the most capable model you have. Many others are better served by something that runs on a phone, or responds in a few milliseconds, or can be run by a small developer who can't afford frontier-level inference. If we only built the biggest models, we'd reach a small set of users. If we only built small ones, we'd stop discovering what's next. So I don't really see it as a trade-off. It's more like one research program with a range of outputs.

r001.rationale: It says many uses are better served by a model that responds in a few milliseconds, supporting smaller models alongside frontier models.

r002.rationale: It explains that a frontier model can act as a teacher through distillation, transferring much of its capability to a smaller model.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think they reinforce each other. You want to push the frontier of what models can do, because there are problems where having the most capable model really matters. And then you also want to make those capabilities available at much lower cost and latency, so people can use them in many more settings.

One of the nice things is that advances at the frontier often help you build better small models. You can use a larger model to help train a smaller one, for example, through distillation. And improvements in efficiency can benefit both ends of that spectrum.

So I don’t think there’s one right model size. If you’re tackling a difficult scientific problem, you might be willing to spend quite a bit of computation. If you want an immediate response on a phone, you have a very different set of constraints. We want to make progress on both.

r001.rationale: It says smaller models make capabilities available at lower latency and gives an immediate phone response as an example.

r002.rationale: It explains that a larger model can help train a smaller one through distillation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they reinforce each other. At the frontier, you’re trying to discover what’s possible—can we make models reason better, tackle harder problems, and work across different kinds of information? That gives you new capabilities, but it also teaches you how to build better models in general.

Then you want to make those capabilities available at much lower cost and latency. A lot of applications don’t need the largest model for every interaction. They need something that responds quickly, is inexpensive enough to use millions of times, or can run on a device. Through things like distillation and improvements in architectures and training, you can bring some of what you learn at the frontier into those smaller models.

So you’re pushing out what’s possible and expanding who can use it. Both are important, and progress in one helps the other.

r001.rationale: The response says many applications need a model that responds quickly, giving low latency as a reason to develop smaller models.

r002.rationale: It explains that frontier learning can be brought into smaller models through distillation, making them more capable.
